rows.title: Quantifying Energy Conversion in Higher-Order Phase Space Density Moments in Plasmas.
rows.abstract: Weakly collisional and collisionless plasmas are typically far from local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), and understanding energy conversion in such systems is a forefront research problem. The standard approach is to investigate changes in internal (thermal) energy and density, but this omits energy conversion that changes any higher-order moments of the phase space density. In this Letter, we calculate from first principles the energy conversion associated with all higher moments of the phase space density for systems not in LTE. Particle-in-cell simulations of collisionless magnetic reconnection reveal that energy conversion associated with higher-order moments can be locally significant. The results may be useful in numerous plasma settings, such as reconnection, turbulence, shocks, and wave-particle interactions in heliospheric, planetary, and astrophysical plasmas.

rows.title: Radiation detection and energy conversion in nuclear reactor environments by hybrid photovoltaic perovskites
rows.abstract: Detection and direct power conversion of high energy and high intensity ionizing radiation could be a key element in next generation nuclear reactor safety systems and space-born devices. For example, the Fukushima catastrophe in 2011 could have been largely prevented if 1\% of the reactor's remnant radiation ($γ$-rays of the nuclear fission) were directly converted within the reactor to electricity to power the water cooling circuit. It is reported here that the hybrid halide perovskite methylammonium lead triiodide could perfectly play the role of a converter. Single crystals were irradiated by a typical shut-down $γ$-spectrum of a nuclear reactor with 7.61E14 Bq activity exhibit a high-efficiency of $γ$-ray to free charge carrier conversion with radiation hardening. The power density of 0.3 mW/kg of methylammonium lead triiodide at 50 Sv/h means a four times higher efficiency than that for silicon-based cells. The material was stable to the limits of the experiment without changing its performance up to 100 Sv/h dose rate and 57 Sv H*(10) ambient total $γ$-dose. Moreover, the γ-shielding performance of methylammonium lead triiodide was found to be superior to both ordinary and barite concrete.

rows.title: scripts for "Phase-dependent mean-flow–wave barotropic energy conversion amplifies turbulence"
rows.abstract: This MATLAB code is used to perform the analyses and generate the main figures for the manuscript titled "Phase-dependent mean-flow–wave barotropic energy conversion amplifies turbulence" (authors: Zhipeng Zhang, Chunhua Qiu, Dake Chen, Changming Dong, Ruixin Huang, Tom Rippeth, Zhao Jing, Xiaolong Yu, Hidekatsu Yamazaki, Huabin Mao, Dongxiao Wang). The code is provided as-is and relies on local files not included here.

rows.title: Short-Wavelength Resonance Dispersive Waves in Gas-Filled Tapered Anti-Resonant Hollow-Core Fibers: Spectra and DW Energy Conversion Efficiency Dataset
rows.abstract: Dispersive-wave (DW) emission within a resonance band of gas-filled anti-resonant hollow-core fibers (AR-HCFs) provides an effective mechanism for ultrafast frequency conversion. For conventional AR-HCFs with a uniform wall thickness, the radiation wavelength is strictly locked by the phase matching condition of the resonance dispersion curve. This makes the emission hardly tunable through gas pressure adjustments alone. Experimentally, the resonance-band DW wavelength for an AR-HCF with a wall thickness of 260 nm was fixed near 550 nm. To actively drive the emission toward shorter wavelengths, we taper the AR-HCF to gradually thin the cladding tube wall along the propagation direction, with a taper ratio of 76%. By altering the phase matching landscape, the tapered AR-HCF shifted the generated DW to 443.3 nm compared with the untapered AR-HCF. We further evaluate the output characteristics across taper ratios of 76%, 70%, and 63%. The results reveal a clear practical trade-off. Ramping up the gas pressure and input energy enhances the conversion efficiency but shifts the emission toward longer wavelengths. Conversely, a larger taper ratio inherently drops the overall conversion efficiency. Ultimately, this tapering strategy provides an effective and flexible way to tune short-wavelength radiation.

rows.title: Theoretical Framework of Dark-to-Light Energy Conversion via Wave Saturation and Phase Transition
rows.abstract: This paper presents a theoretical mechanism for non-linear energy conversion from non-radiative latent states ("Dark Energy") into coherent electromagnetic radiation ("Light") under the framework of Cover Theory. We model the dark continuum as a high-density, non-manifested field that undergoes a threshold-driven phase transition when exposed to localized resonance frequencies. By introducing a critical saturation index S, we establish the exact condition under which latent space oscillations collapse into observable photon emissions.

rows.title: Ti3C2T x MXenes-based flexible materials for electrochemical energy storage and solar energy conversion.
rows.abstract: Over the past decade, two-dimensional (2D) Ti3C2T x MXenes demonstrated attractive characteristics such as high electrical conductivity, tunable layered structure, controllable interfacial chemical composition, high optical transparency, and excellent electromagnetic wave absorption, enabling Ti3C2T x MXenes as promising electrode materials in energy storage devices. Among these devices, flexible energy storage devices have attracted wide attention and developed rapidly due to the synchronously excellent electrochemical and mechanical properties. This review summarizes the recent progress of Ti3C2T x MXenes pertaining to novel material preparation and promising applications in energy storage and conversion including batteries, supercapacitors, solar cells, and solar steam generation. This work aims to provide an in-depth and reasonable understanding of the relationship between the unique nanostructure/chemical composition of Ti3C2T x MXenes and competitive electrochemical properties, which will facilitate the development of 2D Ti3C2T x MXenes for practical energy storage and solar energy conversion devices.

rows.title: Ultrafast wave-particle energy transfer in the collapse of standing whistler waves.
rows.abstract: Efficient energy transfer from electromagnetic waves to ions has been demanded to control laboratory plasmas for various applications and could be useful to understand the nature of space and astrophysical plasmas. However, there exists the severe unsolved problem that most of the wave energy is converted quickly to electrons but not to ions. Here, an energy-to-ion conversion process in overdense plasmas associated with whistler waves is investigated by numerical simulations and a theoretical model. Whistler waves propagating along a magnetic field in space and laboratories often form standing waves by the collision of counter-propagating waves or through the reflection. We find that ions in standing whistler waves acquire a large amount of energy directly from the waves over a short time scale comparable to the wave oscillation period. The thermalized ion temperature increases in proportion to the square of the wave amplitude and becomes much higher than the electron temperature in a wide range of wave-plasma conditions. This efficient ion-heating mechanism applies to various plasma phenomena in space physics and fusion energy sciences.

rows.title: Ultrasonic guided wave propagation across waveguide transitions: energy transfer and mode conversion.
rows.abstract: Ultrasonic guided wave inspection of structures containing adhesively bonded joints requires an understanding of the interaction of guided waves with geometric and material discontinuities or transitions in the waveguide. Such interactions result in mode conversion with energy being partitioned among the reflected and transmitted modes. The step transition between an aluminum layer and an aluminum-adhesive-aluminum multi-layer waveguide is analyzed as a model structure. Dispersion analysis enables assessment of (i) synchronism through dispersion curve overlap and (ii) wavestructure correlation. Mode-pairs in the multi-layer waveguide are defined relative to a prescribed mode in a single layer as being synchronized and having nearly perfect wavestructure matching. Only a limited number of mode-pairs exist, and each has a unique frequency range. A hybrid model based on semi-analytical finite elements and the normal mode expansion is implemented to assess mode conversion at a step transition in a waveguide. The model results indicate that synchronism and wavestructure matching is associated with energy transfer through the step transition, and that the energy of an incident wave mode in a single layer is transmitted almost entirely to the associated mode-pair, where one exists. This analysis guides the selection of incident modes that convert into transmitted modes and improve adhesive joint inspection with ultrasonic guided waves.

rows.title: Wave types and energy conversion of impulse waves generated by landslides into mountain reservoirs.
rows.abstract: Subaerial landslides sliding into shallow water are physically modeled in a three-dimensional wave basin. The generated impulse waves are highly nonlinear, and a large-scale splash zone is formed above the waves. Such impulse wave characteristics are different from those from landslides into deep water that are completely submerged after sliding. The recorded wave profiles included three wave types, namely nonlinear oscillatory wave, nonlinear transition wave and bore-like wave, mainly depending on the relative slide thickness and slide Froude number at impact. Bore-like waves were possible produced only by landslides into shallow water in three-dimensional experiments. The conversion rate of landslide kinetic energy at impact into the wave train energy is 1 to 18%. Energy conversion characteristics are compared with other two- and three-dimensional studies on landslide-generated waves and the results are discussed.

rows.title: An auditable large language model- and retrieval-augmented generation digital quality twin supporting simulation-based validation and safer defect control in Industry 4.0 and 5.0 for production and technology management
rows.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is increasingly considered for supporting production and technology management.In manufacturing quality engineering, LLMs may reduce the cognitive cost of defect analysis, accelerate root-cause diagnostics, and support quality documentation.Still, they can also generate plausible recommendations that are not grounded in evidence.This creates risks of erroneous process interventions, loss of traceability, and non-compliance with artificial intelligence governance requirements.This paper proposes an auditable LLM-augmented digital quality twin (LDQT) architecture that combines an LLM, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), a defect-centric digital quality twin, and human-in-the-loop approval.The architecture is evaluated in a discrete-event simulation of a production stream with stochastic process-drift events and three intervention policies: manual, rule-based, and LDQT.The revised computational study includes Monte Carlo analysis, explicit hypothesis testing, and sensitivity analysis.Under the adopted assumptions of 400 replications and 4000 items per replication, the LDQT scenario indicates an approximately 20% lower mean unit cost of quality and downtime than the manual baseline, as well as a higher first-pass yield.These findings should be interpreted as simulation-based evidence of architectural potential, not as proof of practical effectiveness in a real factory.The contribution is methodological: the study defines the Digital Quality Twin concept and provides metrics for balancing efficiency, auditability, and decision safety in industrial GenAI deployments.

rows.title: Autonomous Laboratories and Foundry Scientific Discovery at the Limit A machine does not discover a mechanism until it creates evidence that could defeat it Core coupling Autonomous experiment x active learning x scientific falsification Research scale 30 linked derivations x 82 chapters x 410 research sections x 200 detailed Research Gates Main result A falsifiable framework for generating, attacking and eliminating process mechanisms rather than confusing recipe optimization with scientific discovery. Series lineage Semiconductor Foundry Technologies x Intelligent Nanomanufacturing - Flagship 20 Publication Abstract This monograph asks whether an autonomous foundry laboratory can do more than optimize an existing recipe. It develops a research architecture in which the system must register competing process mechanisms, identify what its sensors can and cannot distinguish, choose experiments for model discrimination, preserve negative evidence, and issue counterfactual predictions that survive a new tool or fab. Yield improvement, simulation fit, and automation speed are treated as useful engineering outcomes but not as proof of a new mechanism. The central falsifiable proposition is that active experiments chosen to separate rival predictions should reduce the set of observationally equivalent mechanisms and improve preregistered counterfactual forecasts under the same sample, metrology, time, energy, and safety budget as expert DOE and strong safe Bayesian optimization. If the experiment cannot distinguish the models, if failures are selectively forgotten, if the acquisition function exploits a biased proxy, or if cross-tool predictions fail, the scientific claim is narrowed, split, or stopped. Scientific Position and Hard Boundary The work begins with bounded thin-film, deposition, etch, interface, and defect-mechanism challenges in simulation, digital-physical twins, test vehicles, and low-risk equipment states. Autonomous execution is permitted only through typed process intent, equipment capability contracts, explicit authorization, independent metrology, abort logic, and recoverable physical states. No information-gain score may override safety, material irreversibility, chain of custody, environmental obligations, worker protection, or equipment interlocks. Candidate Research Expression Dsci = Delta H of competing models + counterfactual information - sample cost - unsafe risk - hype penalty • Delta H measures reduction in uncertainty over the preregistered mechanism set. • Counterfactual information rewards predictions about interventions or new platforms that were not used for fitting. • Sample cost includes material, metrology, time, energy, and opportunity cost. • Unsafe risk is a hard feasibility concern, not a term that can be purchased by predicted knowledge. • The hype penalty prevents an engineering improvement from being narrated as a causal discovery. Five Layer Research Architecture 01 Competing Mechanism Contract Register rival mechanisms, observable signatures, claim levels, strong baselines, and hard boundaries. 02 Observability and Evidence Graph Map sensors, latent state, calibration ancestry, identifiability, and equivalent model sets. 03 Discriminating Active Experiment Choose controls, interventions, and fidelities for information under sample, energy, and risk budgets. 04 Refutation Memory and Safe Execution Compile typed experiments, preserve failures, detect misspecification, abort safely, and record why models were rejected. 05 Independent Transfer and Successor Choice Demand cross-tool counterfactual predictions, third-party replay, and the right to split, downgrade, or retire a mechanism. Minimum Verifiable Prototype Two process mechanisms are constructed to explain the same historical thin-film or etch observations. Expert DOE, safe Bayesian optimization, and the autonomous discovery policy receive matched samples, metrology, wall time, energy, and safety envelopes. Before the hidden outcomes are revealed, each freezes its hypotheses, predicted signatures, next experiment, acquisition value, uncertainty, and stopping rule. The decisive test is whether independent terminal metrology and a new intervention eliminate or sharply narrow one mechanism, not whether the system merely finds a better recipe. Research Contributions • Separates optimization, prediction, mechanism discrimination, causal support, and cross-platform scientific claims. • Connects observability, identifiability, Fisher information, Bayesian experimental design, causal intervention, and model criticism. • Treats negative results, failed experiments, calibration ancestry, manual corrections, and eliminated models as first-class scientific records. • Maps thirty distinct derivations to chapter, experiment, and Research Gate corridors. • Provides eighty-two chapters with five research pages per chapter: boundary, identifiability, minimum test, adversarial refutation, and successor route.

What the Book Does Not Claim The monograph does not report a completed autonomous fab deployment and does not imply that every process has a uniquely identifiable mechanism. Digital twins can omit decisive state, active learning can exploit a wrong model class, and cross-tool failure may reveal a hidden context variable. Physical deployment requires site-specific engineering validation, material and equipment safety review, worker consultation, cybersecurity, quality-system approval, complete negative-result custody, and accountable human authority. Selected DOI Research Lineage Autonomous laboratory for accelerated materials synthesis: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w Self-driving laboratory and Pareto-front discovery: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-28580-6 Closed-loop materials discovery with Bayesian active learning: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19597-w Performance metrics for self-driving laboratories: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45569-5 Bayesian reaction optimization: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03213-y Autonomous experimentation systems for materials development: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055 Physics-informed machine learning: https://doi.org/10.1038/s42254-021-00314-5 Bayesian calibration of computer models: https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9868.00294 Causal inference in statistics: https://doi.org/10.1214/09-SS057 Concept-drift adaptation survey: https://doi.org/10.1145/2523813 Reproducible research in computational science: https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1213847 File-drawer problem and null results: https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.86.3.638 Suggested English Description A high-density research monograph on autonomous laboratories, active learning, causal experimentation, and falsifiable scientific discovery in semiconductor foundries. The book develops thirty linked derivations, eighty-two chapters, five research sections per chapter, and two hundred detailed Research Gates. It asks whether an AI system can generate competing process mechanisms, choose safe experiments that distinguish their predictions, preserve null and failed results, revise or eliminate models, and make counterfactual forecasts that survive a new tool or fab. The framework distinguishes recipe optimization from mechanism discovery, posterior confidence from identifiability, activity from information, and autonomous execution from scientifically accountable control. It is intended for semiconductor process science, self-driving laboratories, Bayesian experimental design, causal discovery, active learning, digital twins, metrology, reproducibility, and successor-governed research systems. Keywords autonomous laboratory; semiconductor foundry; scientific discovery; active learning; Bayesian experimental design; mechanism discrimination; causal intervention; counterfactual prediction; identifiability; negative results; safe exploration; reproducibility; Research Gates; successor governance AUTONOMOUS LABORATORIES AND FOUNDRY SCIENTIFIC DISCOVERY

rows.title: TITLE SAFETY BARRIERS & REVERSIBLE PROCESS CONTROL FOR NEURAL NANOFABS SUBTITLE A Nonclinical Research Atlas on Process Safety Envelopes, Recipe Provenance, Uncertainty-Aware Metrology, Hybrid Control Barriers, and Reproducible Neural-Interface Wafer Qualification AUTHOR Feng Cheng-en 33 | STARLI Research Works, Institute XXIII ABSTRACT This research atlas asks whether a neural-interface nanofabrication system can preserve a declared safety envelope when manufacturing recipes change, instrument calibration drifts, process chambers retain chemical memory, equipment connectivity fails, and production incentives conflict with physical constraints. Its central scientific distinction is between a control system that generates an action and a production authority that is justified in executing it. The work organizes an interdisciplinary research program into 82 chapters with five single-page sections per chapter, thirty mathematically distinct research lenses, and 200 detailed Research Gates. Across hybrid dynamics, control barrier functions, metrology lineage, virtual metrology, wafer and equipment state tracking, contamination containment, process-history effects, defect-to-function causal analysis, adversarial security, and retirement, each Gate specifies a contestable hypothesis, a preregistered experiment, an established comparison method, a measurable outcome, an explicit failure condition and evidence that a second team could independently reconstruct. The framework is deliberately restricted to digital fab twins, simulated fault injection, dummy wafers, nonhazardous hardware-in-the-loop test rigs, and independently authorized research settings. It does not provide clinically deployable protocols, prove autonomous nanofabrication readiness, or equate neural-device wafer yield with clinical safety or efficacy. DOI-linked literature is used to ground established methods while leaving proposed technology and experimental outcomes clearly unverified. Its research ethic is simple: when evidence weakens, claims contract; when material history is irreversible, software rollback cannot erase physical damage; and when a hard safety predicate fails, throughput optimization must yield to quarantine, human adjudication, or a designed stop. The atlas is intended as a reusable source of falsifiable research questions, not as a certificate of production safety. EDITION NOTE Research Atlas v1.0. Includes 82 chapters, 410 single-page research sections, 30 mathematical lenses, 200 Research Gates, and 16 indexed DOI references. Formal, clinical, and industrial efficacy claims require future independent validation.
