rows.title: Development of Smart Surfaces for Medicine and Biotechnology: Advances in Glass Functionalization through RDRP Techniques.
rows.abstract: All glass represents a material with extremely high utility potential in the development of biomaterials and research tools. Due to a number of its unique properties, such as chemical inertness, thermal stability, and transparency, it can be used in the preparation of hybrid materials for medicine and biotechnology. Such materials can be obtained by grafting polymer brushes from glass surface by reversible deactivation radical polymerization (RDRP) techniques. This paper provides a literature review of the foregoing advances in the development of glass surface modification concepts using atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) and reversible addition-fragmentation chain transfer polymerization (RAFT). These methods are particularly attractive in designing smart coatings because they enable the synthesis of polymers with a well-defined structure and low dispersity. The resulting materials can then serve as antimicrobial surfaces, tools for selective manipulation of cells, and intelligent platforms for creating cell sheets in tissue engineering. Therefore, the idea of glass modification using RDRP techniques appears to be a promising concept for the future in the development of smart materials for various applications.

rows.title: Electrospun glass nanofibers to strengthen polycarbonate plastic glass toward photoluminescent smart materials.
rows.abstract: Electrospun glass nanofibers (GNFs) were used to strengthen polycarbonate (PC) to create long-persistent photoluminescent and fluorescent smart materials such as afterglow concrete and smart window. Physical integration of lanthanide-activated aluminate (LA) nanoparticles (NPs) yielded transparent GNFs@PC smart sheets. Spectral investigations utilizing photoluminescence and CIE Lab parameters were performed to confirm that the translucent appearance of GNFs@PC changed to green when exposed to UV light. This fluorescence activity was quickly reversible for the GNFs@PC hybrids with low concentrations of LANPs, which indicate fluorescence emission. Higher phosphor concentrations in GNFs@PC led to longer-lasting afterglow photoluminescence and slower reversibility. The GNFs@PC hybrids showed an emission band detected at 518 nm upon excitation at 368 nm. The morphological characteristics of LANPs and GNFs were analyzed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM), which revealed sizes of 11-26 nm and 250-300 nm, respectively. GNFs were prepared using electrospinning technology and then used as a roughening agent into PC sheets. Morphological characteristics of GNFs and GNFs@PC smart sheets were examined using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXA), X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The GNFs@PC smart sheets were shown to have enhanced scratch resistance in comparison to LANPs-free PC control sample. Increases in LANPs concentration enhanced both hydrophobicity and UV protection.

rows.title: EPR dosimetry intercomparison using smart phone touch screen glass.
rows.abstract: This paper presents the results of an interlaboratory comparison of retrospective dosimetry using the electron paramagnetic resonance method. The test material used in this exercise was glass coming from the touch screens of smart phones that might be used as fortuitous dosimeters in a large-scale radiological incident. There were 13 participants to whom samples were dispatched, and 11 laboratories reported results. The participants received five calibration samples (0, 0.8, 2, 4, and 10 Gy) and four blindly irradiated samples (0, 0.9, 1.3, and 3.3 Gy). Participants were divided into two groups: for group A (formed by three participants), samples came from a homogeneous batch of glass and were stored in similar setting; for group B (formed by eight participants), samples came from different smart phones and stored in different settings of light and temperature. The calibration curves determined by the participants of group A had a small error and a critical level in the 0.37-0.40-Gy dose range, whereas the curves determined by the participants of group B were more scattered and led to a critical level in the 1.3-3.2-Gy dose range for six participants out of eight. Group A were able to assess the dose within 20 % for the lowest doses (<1.5 Gy) and within 5 % for the highest doses. For group B, only the highest blind dose could be evaluated in a reliable way because of the high critical values involved. The results from group A are encouraging, whereas the results from group B suggest that the influence of environmental conditions and the intervariability of samples coming from different smart phones need to be further investigated. An alongside conclusion is that the protocol was easily transferred to participants making a network of laboratories in case of a mass casualty event potentially feasible.

rows.title: Fabrication of pH-Responsive Zn2+-Releasing Glass Particles for Smart Antibacterial Restoratives.
rows.abstract: The on-demand release of antibacterial components due to pH variations caused by acidogenic/cariogenic bacteria is a possible design for smart antibacterial restorative materials. This study aimed to fabricate pH-responsive Zn2+-releasing glass particles and evaluate their solubilities, ion-releasing characteristics, and antibacterial properties in vitro. Three kinds of silicate-based glass particles containing different molar ratios of Zn (PG-1: 25.3; PG-2: 34.6; PG-3: 42.7 mol%) were fabricated. Each particle was immersed in a pH-adjusted medium, and the solubility and concentration of the released ions were determined. To evaluate the antibacterial effect, Streptococcus mutans was cultured in the pH-adjusted medium in the presence of each particle, and the bacterial number was counted. The solubility and concentration of Zn2+ released in the medium increased with a decrease in medium pH. PG-3 with a greater content of Zn demonstrated higher concentrations of released Zn2+ compared with PG-1 and PG-2. PG-2 exhibited bactericidal effects at pH 5.1, whereas PG-3 demonstrated bactericidal effects at pH values of 5.1 and 6.1, indicating that PG-3 was effective at inhibiting S. mutans even under slightly acidic conditions. The glass particle with 42.7 mol% Zn may be useful for developing smart antibacterial restoratives that contribute to the prevention of diseases such as caries on root surfaces with lower acid resistance.

rows.title: From glass ceilings to smart systems: Investigating the link between gender-inclusive corporate boards and AI transformation in banking
rows.abstract: This study examines the association between gender-inclusive boards and AI adoption in Nigeria's banking sector, with particular attention to board leadership, regulatory compliance and risk management. Using a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected through structured questionnaires administered to 100 employees of listed Nigerian banks between February and June 2025. The population of the study consists of all 12 commercial banks listed on the Nigerian exchange Group (NGX). A purposive sampling technique was used to select 5 banks based on total assets and market capitalisation. A total of 100 employees participated in the survey, representing approximately 20 respondents from each bank. Respondents were drawn from executive management, customer service and risk/compliance and IT units. Board-level variables such as gender inclusion and board leadership were obtained from the corporate governance disclosures of sampled banks which were then matched with employee survey responses from the corresponding bank. Thus, employee perceptions of AI adoption, regulatory compliance and risk balance were analysed alongside bank-specific governance characteristics. Multiple regression model was used to estimate the data. The results revealed significant positive associations between gender inclusion (β = 0.297, p < 0.05), board leadership (β = 0.331, p < 0.05), regulatory compliance (β = 0.309, p < 0.05), risk management (β = 0.115, p < 0.05) and AI adoption, with the regression model explaining 74.1% of the variation in AI uptake across sampled banks. The findings suggest that banks with stronger gender representation on boards tend to report higher levels of AI adoption and stronger governance practices. The study concludes that gender diversity on boards enhances banks’ capacity to navigate digital transformation responsibly. Therefore, the study recommends targeted training for board members, policy incentives for diversity, and integrated compliance mechanisms to ensure sustainable and inclusive AI-driven innovation in the financial sector.

rows.title: Glass Fiber Reinforced Concrete as a Durable and Enhanced Material for Structural and Architectural Elements in Smart City-A Review.
rows.abstract: The article highlights that glass fiber reinforced concretes (GFRC) can meet the requirements of Smart City better than ordinary concretes. The comprehensive discussion on GFRC composition is presented together with the review of glass fibers' influence on various concrete properties. First of all, because of their bridging abilities, they can limit the width, length, and total area of cracks. Additionally, GFRC are characterized by enhanced tensile, flexural, and splitting strength; impact, abrasion, spalling, fire, and freeze-thaw resistance as well as ductility, toughness, and permeability. All of this positively influences the mechanical behavior, durability, and corrosion resistance of concrete elements. Moreover, decreased thermal conductivity allows for better energy performance from the building's point of view. This results in cheaper structures both in manufacturing and maintaining even though GFRC are more expensive materials. However, mechanical properties enhance as long as sufficient workability and uniform fiber distribution are assured. From the environmental point of view, GFRC are eco-friendlier materials than ordinary concretes since their application can decrease the emission of CO2 by 17%. The article also describes the GFRC application fields and emphasizes the possibility of the creation of not only structural elements mainly intended for load transferring but also elements accompanying the building process, as well as elements of small architecture that make public spaces more attractive, durable, and safer. Owing to greater design and shaping freedom, GFRC can also better fulfill the needs of habitants of Smart City.

rows.title: Microleakage of Silver-Modified Atraumatic Restorative Technique (SMART) Restorations Using Silver Diammine Fluoride and High-Viscosity Glass Ionomer.
rows.abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to investigate the microleakage of atraumatic glass ionomer restorations with and without silver diammine fluoride (SDF) application. Restorations with SDF are termed silver-modified atraumatic restorations (SMART). Methods: Sixty carious extracted permanent teeth were randomly allocated to two SMART groups and two control groups (n equals 15 per group) for a total of four groups. After selective caries removal, test specimens were treated with 38 percent SDF and polyacrylic acid conditioner was applied and rinsed; teeth were restored with Fuji IX GP® glass ionomer (n equals 15) or with SMART Advantage™ glass ionomer (SAGI; n equals 15). For control groups, specimens were restored with their respective GI material after selective caries removal, both without SDF. Restored teeth were placed in Dulbecco's Phosphate-Buffered Saline solution at 37 degrees Celsius for 24 hours. Teeth were thermocycled between five and 55 degrees Celsius for 1,000 cycles, stained with two percent basic fuchsin, sectioned, and visually inspected for microleakage utilizing stereomicroscopy on a four-point scale. Data were statistically analyzed using Kruskal-Wallis one-way analysis of variance on ranks using Dunn's method (P<0.05). Results: Microleakage between the two SMART restoration groups was insignificant. SAGI alone demonstrated significantly more microleakage than all other groups. There was no statistical significance between the Fuji IX GP® control group and the two SMART restoration groups. Conclusions: This in vitro study indicated that silver diammine fluoride placed before glass ionomer restoration does not increase microleakage. Polyacrylic acid may be used after SDF placement without increasing microleakage.

rows.title: Nb-Doped VO 2 -Based Coatings on Glass: Substrate Effects, Thermochromic Performance, and an Effective Transition Temperature for Smart-Glazing Applications
rows.abstract: High Resolution Image Download MS PowerPoint Slide Niobium-doped VO 2 thin films were deposited on soda-lime and borosilicate glass substrates to investigate the coupled effects of dopant concentration, substrate chemistry, and thermal processing on microstructure, thermochromic performance, and metal–insulator transition (MIT) kinetics. Coatings with nominal Nb contents of 3, 4.5, and 6 at. % were fabricated using controlled mono- and multilayer codeposition strategies followed by rapid thermal annealing. Structural and morphological analyses confirm VO 2 (M) as the dominant phase on both substrates, while revealing a strong substrate-dependent stability of secondary phases driven by Na diffusion, especially in soda-lime glass. Advanced scanning-transmission electron microscopy image and spectroscopic-related techniques demonstrate that Nb exhibits a less homogeneous spatial distribution than other dopants (such as W) under comparable processing conditions, leading to compositional modulations and multistep MIT behavior, particularly on soda-lime substrates. In contrast, borosilicate glass enables enhanced grain coalescence, reduced Na-induced phase instability, and a more uniform Nb incorporation. These microstructural differences directly impact the optical response. Borosilicate-supported coatings exhibit a more favorable balance between luminous transmittance ( T lum ) and solar modulation efficiency (Δ T sol ), while films on soda-lime glass show a progressive degradation of Δ T sol at higher Nb contents. Despite a lower T c reduction efficiency compared to W, Nb doping preserves or even improves T lum at elevated concentrations. Finally, an application-oriented effective transition temperature, T eff, is proposed as a more realistic metric for assessing the suitability of VO 2 -based coatings for smart-glazing applications.

rows.title: New Wearable Computers Move Ahead: Google Glass and Smart Wigs.
Optimizing smart window glass selection to address contemporary environmental challenges using fuzzy multi-criteria decision analytics
rows.abstract: In recent times, the world has been dealing with multiple environmental crises, including rising global temperatures, excessive energy consumption, elevated urban temperatures, and increasing carbon emissions from the building industry. As buildings have a significant impact on energy use, it is essential to address these challenges. In particular, window glass plays a significant role in controlling heat transfer, regulating indoor temperatures and reducing the dependence on artificial cooling. Therefore, selecting the most suitable energy-efficient glass has become crucial for sustainable development. Construction technology has introduced specialized glass materials for windows, including smart window technologies that automatically regulate heat and light. This study aims to identify the most suitable energy-efficient glass using a fuzzy multi-criteria decision-making method. Here, eight different alternatives are evaluated against eleven conflicting criteria classified as performance enhancing criteria (PEC) and performance reducing criteria (PRC). The Simultaneous Evaluation of Criteria and Alternative (SECA) method is employed for determining criteria weights, and the COmbinative Distance-based ASsessment (CODAS) approach is utilized to evaluate ranks of the alternatives. To ensure reliability and robustness, the study performed comparative and sensitivity analyses. The results indicate that electrochromic (EC) windows (A4) are the most suitable smart glazing technology among the considered alternatives. The results help urban planners and architects select energy-efficient glass for smart windows.

rows.title: Preparation of Lanthanide Aluminate and Glass Nanofiber-Supported Polyacrylonitrile Plastic Smart Window.
rows.abstract: Lanthanides are a common component in glass windows for smart products. However, glasses are fragile and inflexible, corrosive to alkali, and costly, whereas plastics are cheap, durable, and safe. Herein, afterglow and photochromic smart plastic windows were developed by reinforcing polyacrylonitrile (PAN) with electrospun glass nanofibers (GNF; 65-125 nm). Transparent films with photoluminescence properties were introduced by physically immobilizing rare-earth doped aluminate nanoparticles (REAN; 7-13 nm) into a composite of GNF@PAN. When irradiated with ultraviolet light, the GNF@PAN samples showed a change in color from transparent to green as proved by coloration parameters and photoluminescence spectra. An emission band was detected at 518 nm upon excitation at 365 nm. The morphology of the photoluminescent hybrids was investigated by different analytical techniques. The scratch resistance of GNF@PAN was significantly enhanced when the REAN content was increased. With low concentration levels of REAN, GNF@PAN quickly reversed photochromism to signify fluorescence emission. GNF@PAN with high REAN concentrations showed afterglow emission via prolonged emission in the dark. The photoluminescent hybrids showed enhanced superhydrophobic and ultraviolet blocking upon increasing the phosphor content. The photoluminescent plastics displayed an improved hydrophobicity from 139.1° to 150.8° when the phosphor content was increased.

rows.title: Smart ceramic coating from lanthanide aluminate-encapsulated silica nanoparticle-immobilized electrospun glass nanofiber-reinforced epoxy nanocomposite
SMART: Silver diamine fluoride reduces microtensile bond strength of glass ionomer cement to sound and artificial caries-affected dentin.
rows.abstract: Silver-modified atraumatic restorative technique (SMART) is an emerging restorative technique; however, the effect of silver diamine fluoride (SDF) application on the bond strength of glass ionomer cement (GIC) is unknown. This study aimed to determine if SDF application to sound and artificial caries-affected dentin (ACAD) immediately prior to GIC restoration affected microtensile bond strength (µTBS). Caries was induced on extracted molars using a pH-cycling protocol that was validated against natural caries (similar µTBS). Dentin surfaces were treated with 38% SDF, control groups with de-ionized water and immediately restored. Beam-shaped specimens were sectioned and subjected to tensile forces for µTBS determination. Two hundred and eighty-seven specimens from 40 teeth were tested. SDF application significantly (p<0.001) reduced µTBS in sound dentin (19.00±8.20 MPa vs. 14.60±6.68 MPa), while no difference was found in ACAD. No difference was found in failure mode among groups. For SMART, SDF application on sound dentin before immediate GIC restoration may decrease bond strength.

rows.title: Stimulus-responsive smart bioactive glass composites for repair of complex tissue defects.
rows.abstract: Smart biomaterials with active environmental responsiveness have attracted widespread attention in recent years. Previous studies on bioactive glass (BG) have mainly focused on the property of bioactivity, while little attention has been paid to the property of smart response of BG. Herein, we propose the concept of Smart Bioactive Glass Composites (SBGC) which are capable of actively responding to the endogenous disease microenvironment or exogenous physical stimuli, thereby enabling active treatment of tissue defect sites and ultimately promoting tissue regeneration. In this review, the response characteristics of SBGC to different internal and external environments are described. Subsequently, the applications of SBGC in complex tissue defect repair of tumors, infections, and diabetes are reviewed. By deeply analyzing the recent progress of SBGC in different fields, this review will point out the direction for the research of next-generation BG.

rows.title: The energy saving potential of a novel smart photochromic glass film for a model office across various European climates
Transparent perovskite dual-color films via laser-induced polymerization-crystallization with anion migration blocking for smart display glass
What Is Driving the Growth of Inorganic Glass in Smart Materials and Opto-Electronic Devices?
rows.abstract: Inorganic glass is a transparent functional material and one of the few materials that keeps leading innovation. In the last decades, inorganic glass was integrated into opto-electronic devices such as optical fibers, semiconductors, solar cells, transparent photovoltaic devices, or photonic crystals and in smart materials applications such as environmental, pharmaceutical, and medical sensors, reinforcing its influence as an essential material and providing potential growth opportunities for the market. Moreover, inorganic glass is the only material that is 100% recyclable and can incorporate other industrial offscourings and/or residues to be used as raw materials. Over time, inorganic glass experienced an extensive range of fabrication techniques, from traditional melting-quenching (with an immense diversity of protocols) to chemical vapor deposition (CVD), physical vapor deposition (PVD), and wet chemistry routes as sol-gel and solvothermal processes. Additive manufacturing (AM) was recently added to the list. Bulks (3D), thin/thick films (2D), flexible glass (2D), powders (2D), fibers (1D), and nanoparticles (NPs) (0D) are examples of possible inorganic glass architectures able to integrate smart materials and opto-electronic devices, leading to added-value products in a wide range of markets. In this review, selected examples of inorganic glasses in areas such as: (i) magnetic glass materials, (ii) solar cells and transparent photovoltaic devices, (iii) photonic crystal, and (iv) smart materials are presented and discussed.

rows.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Secured Power Grid Protocol for Smart City.
rows.abstract: Due to the modern power system's rapid development, more scattered smart grid components are securely linked into the power system by encircling a wide electrical power network with the underpinning communication system. By enabling a wide range of applications, such as distributed energy management, system state forecasting, and cyberattack security, these components generate vast amounts of data that automate and improve the efficiency of the smart grid. Due to traditional computer technologies' inability to handle the massive amount of data that smart grid systems generate, AI-based alternatives have received a lot of interest. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) will be specifically developed in this study to address this issue by incorporating the adaptively time-developing energy system's attributes to enhance the model of the dynamic properties of contemporary Smart Grid (SG) that are impacted by Revised Encoding Scheme (RES) or system reconfiguration to differentiate LSTM changes & real-time threats. More specifically, we provide a federated instructional strategy for consumer sharing of power data to Power Grid (PG) that is supported by edge clouds, protects consumer privacy, and is communication-efficient. They then design two optimization problems for Energy Data Owners (EDO) and energy service operations, as well as a local information assessment method in Federated Learning (FL) by taking non-independent and identically distributed (IID) effects into consideration. The test results revealed that LSTM had a longer training duration, four hidden levels, and higher training loss than other models. The provided method works incredibly well in several situations to identify FDIA. The suggested approach may successfully induce EDOs to employ high-quality local models, increase the payout of the ESP, and decrease task latencies, according to extensive simulations, which are the last points. According to the verification results, every assault sample could be effectively recognized utilizing the current detection methods and the LSTM RNN-based structure created by Smart.

rows.title: Capacity Estimation for Vehicle-to-Grid Frequency Regulation Services with Smart Charging Mechanism
rows.abstract: Due to various green initiatives, renewable energy will be massively incorporated into the future smart grid. However, the intermittency of the renewables may result in power imbalance, thus adversely affecting the stability of a power system. Frequency regulation may be used to maintain the power balance at all times. As electric vehicles (EVs) become popular, they may be connected to the grid to form a vehicle-to-grid (V2G) system. An aggregation of EVs can be coordinated to provide frequency regulation services. However, V2G is a dynamic system where the participating EVs come and go independently. Thus it is not easy to estimate the regulation capacities for V2G. In a preliminary study, we modeled an aggregation of EVs with a queueing network, whose structure allows us to estimate the capacities for regulation-up and regulation-down, separately. The estimated capacities from the V2G system can be used for establishing a regulation contract between an aggregator and the grid operator, and facilitating a new business model for V2G. In this paper, we extend our previous development by designing a smart charging mechanism which can adapt to given characteristics of the EVs and make the performance of the actual system follow the analytical model.

rows.title: Coordinated Management of Residential Batteries and Vehicle-to-Grid Resources Under Dynamic Electricity Pricing in a Smart Community Microgrid
rows.abstract: The increasing integration of photovoltaic (PV) systems, battery energy storage systems (BESSs), and electric vehicles (EVs) is transforming residential electricity networks into flexible community microgrids. However, intermittent renewable generation and mismatches between generation and demand require effective energy management strategies for reliable and economical operation. This paper presents a dynamic pricing-based Energy Management System (EMS) for a residential PV microgrid comprising 19 households with a total rooftop PV capacity of 76 kW, distributed battery storage rated at 9.6 kWh per household, and 19 Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G)-enabled EVs with 50 kWh battery capacity each. The proposed EMS integrates PV generation data obtained from PVsyst, residential load profiles, dynamic electricity pricing, and coordinated control of household batteries, EV charging/discharging, V2G operation, and grid interactions. A rule-based scheduling framework is employed to improve renewable energy utilization, reduce electricity procurement costs, and enhance overall microgrid performance under predefined operational and price-based decision rules. Hourly-resolution simulations were conducted over an extended operating period to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. The results achieved a PV self-consumption rate of 86.9%, community energy self-sufficiency of 63.6%, and PV energy coverage of 87.9%. The coordinated storage operation resulted in 34,732 kWh of battery charging energy and 30,018 kWh of discharged energy, with an average battery efficiency of 86.4%. Grid imports and exports were 27,671 kWh and 10,015 kWh, respectively, yielding an export-to-import ratio of 0.36. Transformer loading was maintained at 12.8% of its rated capacity, indicating secure transformer operation with loading well below the rated capacity. Overall, the proposed rule-based EMS improves renewable energy utilization, grid flexibility, and operational performance, providing a practical approach for managing distributed energy resources in residential community microgrids.

rows.title: Enhancing Observability in Distribution Grids using Smart Meter Data
rows.abstract: Due to limited metering infrastructure, distribution grids are currently challenged by observability issues. On the other hand, smart meter data, including local voltage magnitudes and power injections, are communicated to the utility operator from grid buses with renewable generation and demand-response programs. This work employs grid data from metered buses towards inferring the underlying grid state. To this end, a coupled formulation of the power flow problem (CPF) is put forth. Exploiting the high variability of injections at metered buses, the controllability of solar inverters, and the relative time-invariance of conventional loads, the idea is to solve the non-linear power flow equations jointly over consecutive time instants. An intuitive and easily verifiable rule pertaining to the locations of metered and non-metered buses on the physical grid is shown to be a necessary and sufficient criterion for local observability in radial networks. To account for noisy smart meter readings, a coupled power system state estimation (CPSSE) problem is further developed. Both CPF and CPSSE tasks are tackled via augmented semi-definite program relaxations. The observability criterion along with the CPF and CPSSE solvers are numerically corroborated using synthetic and actual solar generation and load data on the IEEE 34-bus benchmark feeder.

rows.title: Optimal micro-grid battery scheduling within a comprehensive smart pricing scheme.
rows.abstract: The challenge of optimizing battery operating revenue while mitigating aging costs remains inadequately addressed in current literature. This paper introduces a novel cost-benefit approach for scheduling battery energy storage systems (BESS) within microgrids (MGs) that features smart grid attributes. The proposed comprehensive approach accounts for fluctuations of real-time pricing, demand charge tariffs, and battery degradation cost. Using the dynamic programming technique, a novel high-speed BESS scheduling optimization algorithm that incorporates a LiFePO4 battery degradation cost model is developed, achieving substantial monthly operational cost savings for the MG with a fine-grained sampling interval of nine minutes and execution time under one minute. The algorithm utilizes day-ahead forecasts for MG load profiles and photovoltaic output power, enabling the prediction of BESS's optimal power profile a day in advance. The algorithm's rapid execution enables real-time adaptability, allowing BESS scheduling to dynamically respond to grid fluctuations. The proposed approach outperforms existing methods in the literature, delivering MG operational cost savings ranging from 33.6% to 94.8% across various scenarios. Consequently, this approach enhances MG operational efficiency and provides significant cost savings.

rows.title: REAL-TIME PARTIAL DISCHARGE MONITORING AS AN EARLY-WARNING SYSTEM FOR SMART GIS SUBSTATIONS IN SAUDI ARABIA: PREVENTING FAILURES AND IMPROVING GRID RESILIENCE
rows.abstract: Gas - insulated switchgear (GIS) occupies a strategically important position in compact, high-voltage substations, yet concealed insulation defects can develop before conventional protection operates. Partial discharge (PD) monitoring offers a means of recognising such deterioration during service, although detection alone does not establish failure imminence or guarantee outage avoidance. This critical review evaluates advances published between 2020 and 2025 in electromagnetic, acoustic, optical and gas-based PD sensing, alongside localisation, analytical classification and operational decision support. It synthesises the evidence through an engineering chain linking physical defects, trustworthy measurements, interpreted condition, intervention and electricity-service outcomes. The proposed framework differentiates signal detection from defect diagnosis and separates equipment reliability from system resilience. Particular consideration is given to intermittent discharges, sensor ageing, domain shift between laboratories and substations, alarm governance, cybersecurity and Saudi environmental and network conditions. The review argues for calibrated, multimodal monitoring with uncertainty - aware alarms and documented maintenance decisions, rather than unconditional reliance on automated classifications.

rows.title: Transforming the electrical grid: the role of AI in advancing smart, sustainable, and secure energy systems
rows.abstract: The evolution of the electrical grid from its early centralized structure to today’s advanced “smart grid” reflects significant technological progress. Early grids, designed for simple power delivery from large plants to consumers, faced challenges in efficiency, reliability, and scalability. Over time, the grid has transformed into a decentralized network driven by innovative technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI). AI has become instrumental in enhancing efficiency, security, and resilience by enabling real-time data analysis, predictive maintenance, demand-response optimization, and automated fault detection, thereby improving overall operational efficiency. This paper examines the evolution of the electrical grid, tracing its transition from early limitations to the methodologies adopted in present smart grids for addressing those challenges. Current smart grids leverage AI to optimize energy management, predict faults, and seamlessly integrate electric vehicles (EVs), reducing transmission losses and improving performance. However, these advancements are not without limitations. Present grids remain vulnerable to cyberattacks, necessitating the adoption of more robust methodologies and advanced technologies for future grids. Looking forward, emerging technologies such as Digital Twin (DT) models, the Internet of Energy (IoE), and decentralized grid management are set to redefine grid architectures. These advanced technologies enable real-time simulations, adaptive control, and enhanced human–machine collaboration, supporting dynamic energy distribution and proactive risk management. Integrating AI with advanced energy storage, renewable resources, and adaptive access control mechanisms will ensure future grids are resilient, sustainable, and responsive to growing energy demands. This study emphasizes AI’s transformative role in addressing the challenges of the early grid, enhancing the capabilities of the present smart grid, and shaping a secure, efficient, and adaptive next-generation grid aligned with future needs.

rows.title: Two-Timescale Stochastic Dispatch of Smart Distribution Grids
rows.abstract: Smart distribution grids should efficiently integrate stochastic renewable resources while effecting voltage regulation. The design of energy management schemes is challenging, one of the reasons being that energy management is a multistage problem where decisions are not all made at the same timescale and must account for the variability during real-time operation. The joint dispatch of slow- and fast-timescale controls in a smart distribution grid is considered here. The substation voltage, the energy exchanged with a main grid, and the generation schedules for small diesel generators have to be decided on a slow timescale; whereas optimal photovoltaic inverter setpoints are found on a more frequent basis. While inverter and looser voltage regulation limits are imposed at all times, tighter bus voltage constraints are enforced on the average or in probability, thus enabling more efficient renewable integration. Upon reformulating the two-stage grid dispatch as a stochastic convex-concave problem, two distribution-free schemes are put forth. An average dispatch algorithm converges provably to the optimal two-stage decisions via a sequence of convex quadratic programs. Its non-convex probabilistic alternative entails solving two slightly different convex problems and is numerically shown to converge. Numerical tests on a real-world distribution feeder verify that both novel data-driven schemes yield lower costs over competing alternatives.

rows.title: ASSURANCE ENGINEERING FOR AUTONOMOUS QUANTUM–NANO HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE AT THE LIMIT Measurement Trust × Clinical Authority × Recoverable Infrastructure This exploratory research monograph investigates how safety evidence could be constructed for future autonomous quantum–nano health infrastructure without confusing physical sensing accuracy, AI recommendations, professional permission, clinical effectiveness, and regulatory authorization. The central research question is whether every consequential recommendation can be reconstructed from traceable measurements, interpreted with declared uncertainty, subjected to legally and professionally valid human authorization, and linked to an independently verified safe-state and recovery pathway. The monograph is a tri-coupled synthesis of three prior mother architectures: Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 72–79, for distributed-agent security and operational fault tolerance; Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, particularly chapters 25–82, for bounded decision authority, recoverable intervention architecture and successor-ready safety evidence; and Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 65–73, for reference trust, bounded calibration, serviceability and governance. These mother architectures supply research methods and constraints. Their combination does not demonstrate that the integrated technology is clinically effective, medically approved, or already deployed. Across 82 chapters and 12 separately paginated research studies per chapter, the work develops a versioned Claim–Argument–Evidence architecture for non-clinical quantum–nano health systems. It examines raw-to-result metrology, shared-reference errors, uncertainty propagation, model calibration and digital twins, operator authentication, explicit professional authority envelopes, fail-closed control, verification, manual override, classical backup, malicious or degraded devices, alarm fatigue, incident replay, recovery closure, lifecycle economics, fairness, privacy and independent cross-site reconstruction. Thirty physical and mathematical derivation plates separate established relations and their validity conditions from the book's unvalidated research heuristics. The NQ-14 deployment expression is a conceptual four-gate test: adequate evidence, valid authority, verified recovery and compliance with the applicable regulatory pathway are jointly necessary. Its Boolean structure is not a proof of safety or legal status, nor can a composite index replace consequence-specific vetoes. Every chapter offers a candidate model and a three-dimensional evidence geometry. The intended verification environment uses synthetic observations and hardware-in-the-loop non-clinical simulations. Proposed trials inject inaccurate calibration references, correlated sensor faults, operator overload, unauthorized delegation, model and firmware drift, unavailable classical backup and simultaneous communication failures. Outcomes are compared with strong classical-only and human-supervised baselines under a declared test domain; unauthorized high-consequence action, missing provenance or unrecoverable state is a rejection condition even when prediction accuracy rises. The volume concludes with 200 independent Research Gates and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each has an equation egg drawn from an existing physical or mathematical relationship and accompanied by a validity boundary. An accompanying Research Gates spreadsheet preserves gate questions, tests, vetoes, provenance, assurance-case claims, human authority matrices and recovery evidence so that later laboratories may reproduce, refute, revise, split or retire the proposals. SCIENTIFIC, CLINICAL AND REGULATORY BOUNDARY: This is an exploratory, non-clinical, partly template-assisted research architecture. It reports no clinical trials, medical outcomes, validation of autonomous quantum–nano therapy or regulatory clearance. AI models do not obtain permission to diagnose or treat patients through inference quality. Clinical uses would require qualified professional oversight, intended-use evidence, independent validation, ethical governance and applicable jurisdiction-specific regulatory processes. Relevant context includes BIPM/JCGM metrology guidance, IMDRF SaMD clinical evaluation documents and FDA guidance on AI device software change management, none of which is presented as approval of the proposed platform. The thirty derivation plates are research-level derivation sketches rather than complete textbook proofs; the 233 numbered equation eggs are not discoveries of 233 new physical laws. Feng Cheng-en (33) × Starli STARLI Nano–Quantum Tri-Coupling Research Series | Flagship 14 | 2026

It examines raw-to-result metrology, shared-reference errors, uncertainty propagation, model calibration and digital twins, operator authentication, explicit professional authority envelopes, fail-closed control, verification, manual override, classical backup, malicious or degraded devices, alarm fatigue, incident replay, recovery closure, lifecycle economics, fairness, privacy and independent cross-site reconstruction. Thirty physical and mathematical derivation plates separate established relations and their validity conditions from the book’s unvalidated research heuristics. The NQ-14 deployment expression is a conceptual four-gate test: adequate evidence, valid authority, verified recovery and compliance with the applicable regulatory pathway are jointly necessary. Its Boolean structure is not a proof of safety or legal status, nor can a composite index replace consequence-specific vetoes. Every chapter offers a candidate model and a three-dimensional evidence geometry. The intended verification environment uses synthetic observations and hardware-in-the-loop non-clinical simulations. Proposed trials inject inaccurate calibration references, correlated sensor faults, operator overload, unauthorized delegation, model and firmware drift, unavailable classical backup and simultaneous communication failures. Outcomes are compared with strong classical-only and human-supervised baselines under a declared test domain; unauthorized high-consequence action, missing provenance or unrecoverable state is a rejection condition even when prediction accuracy rises. Each has an equation egg drawn from an existing physical or mathematical relationship and accompanied by a validity boundary. An accompanying Research Gates spreadsheet preserves gate questions, tests, vetoes, provenance, assurance-case claims, human authority matrices and recovery evidence so that later laboratories may reproduce, refute, revise, split or retire the proposals. AI models do not obtain permission to diagnose or treat patients through inference quality. Clinical uses would require qualified professional oversight, intended-use evidence, independent validation, ethical governance and applicable jurisdiction-specific regulatory processes. Constructing a cohesive pattern for collective navigation based on a swarm of robotics.
rows.abstract: Swarm robotics carries out complex tasks beyond the power of simple individual robots. Limited capabilities of sensing and communication by simple mobile robots have been essential inspirations for aggregation tasks. Aggregation is crucial behavior when performing complex tasks in swarm robotics systems. Many difficulties are facing the aggregation algorithm. These difficulties are as such: this algorithm has to work under the restrictions of no information about positions, no central control, and only local information interaction among robots. This paper proposed a new aggregation algorithm. This algorithm combined with the wave algorithm to achieve collective navigation and the recruitment strategy. In this work, the aggregation algorithm consists of two main phases: the searching phase, and the surrounding phase. The execution time of the proposed algorithm was analyzed. The experimental results showed that the aggregation time in the proposed algorithm was significantly reduced by 41% compared to other algorithms in the literature. Moreover, we analyzed our results using a one-way analysis of variance. Also, our results showed that the increasing swarm size significantly improved the performance of the group.

Its core three-coupling is Reference Portability × Cross-Site Comparison × Versioned Provenance. It joins the methodological lineages of Swarm Manufacturing & Robotic Matter at the Limit, Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, and Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit.

rows.title: Dynamic Adaptation of Communication Topology in Robotic Swarms Based on Local Graph k-Connectivity
rows.abstract: Ensuring the stability of the communication structure in robotic swarms with limited communication range requires the development of effective mechanisms for adapting the interaction topology between agents. In dynamically changing environments, conventional fixed-topology approaches prove inadequate, necessitating adaptive solutions that function without comprehensive network knowledge. This study investigates a dynamic connectivity graph management method grounded in local node k-connectivity metrics, which quantify the minimum number of agents whose removal would isolate a given node from the network. We propose an algorithm for selecting control agents based on degree centrality criteria while accounting for the structure of connected graph components, implemented within a modular software environment for reproducible testing on double integrator and quadcopter models. Computations proceed in a decentralized manner using local measurements, minimizing communication channel load and enabling scalability as group size increases. Experimental evaluation on systems ranging from 10 to 100 agents demonstrates that the adaptive approach improves connectivity preservation probability from 64 % to 88 % under conditions with 20 % malicious agents in sparse topologies, while the average local k-connectivity increases from 2.3 to 3.8 for k-nearest neighbor scenarios with k = 3. Computational complexity analysis confirms the method’s scalability, with graph update times of 15—45 ms for systems up to 100 agents at a 20 Hz sampling frequency. The low latency of topology calculations enables integration into real-time control loops for micro-UAV and ground platform onboard controllers. Future work may incorporate data transmission delay models and kinematic constraints of physical robots to facilitate field testing. These findings advance decentralized control theory for distributed systems and provide a foundation for designing fault-tolerant robotic swarm architectures.

rows.title: Field-Driven Out-of-Equilibrium Collective Patterns for Swarm Micro-Robotics.
rows.abstract: Soft robotics has been rapidly advancing, offering significant improvements over traditional rigid robotic systems through the use of compliant materials that enhance adaptability and interaction with the environment. However, current approaches face critical challenges, including the reliance on complex "top-down" fabrication techniques and the difficulty of wireless powering and control at the microscale. Swarm robotics introduces a paradigm shift, leveraging collective dynamics to achieve cooperative and adaptable behaviors among multiple robotic units. Inspired by nature, this "bottom-up" approach enables swarm robots to execute task-specific reconfigurations, enhancing flexibility and robustness. Field-driven active colloids emerge as a promising platform for swarm microrobotics, capable of self-propulsion and self-organization into dynamic collective patterns under external field excitation and manipulation. These systems mimic biologically inspired swarm behaviors, such as flocking and vortex formation, providing a versatile foundation for designing innovative swarm microrobots. This review discusses the principles of electric and magnetic field-driven collective self-organization, focusing on the particle dynamics, the emergence of collective swarm patterns, and illustrative examples of functional swarm microrobots. It concludes with future perspectives on harnessing these systems for adaptive, scalable, and multifunctional microrobotic applications.

rows.title: From nature to robotics: insights of animals collective behaviors on the development of swarm intelligence and multi-robot systems.
rows.abstract: The collective behaviors observed in marine, terrestrial, and aerial animals, exhibiting fascinating phenomena that emerge from simple interaction rules among individuals, provide valuable inspiration for swarm intelligence (SI) and robotics. This paper summarizes foraging, hunting, following and aggregation four typical animal collective behaviors and explores their relationship with SI. Building on this, we present the state of the art of research efforts to explore the use of SI in addressing multi-robot coordination problems, focusing on three key topics: spatial organization, navigation, and collective decision-making. These insights are based on research indexed in the Web of Science database. Through the analysis of key aspects, this article identifies current challenges, future development directions, and application prospects from three perspectives: animals, SI and robots. This review serves as an overview for scholars and professionals in the field of multi-robot systems.

rows.title: HGRL: A heterogeneous graph-based reinforcement learning framework for robotic swarm applications
rows.abstract: Graph neural networks provide a structured approach for representing entities and their relationships in multi-agent systems. In this paper, we propose a heterogeneous graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework, termed HGRL, to support decision-making in robotic swarms. HGRL represents the interactions among agents and environmental entities using heterogeneous graphs. Unlike graph-based MARL methods that retain conventional transition tuples, HGRL encodes state–action transitions as variable-size heterogeneous graph objects and preserves this representation during experience replay and actor-critic optimization. This graph-based formulation allows changes in the numbers and types of agents and environmental entities without restructuring fixed-width experience entries. A graph-based multi-agent soft actor-critic agent is developed to demonstrate HGRL for UAV swarm collaborative navigation, using attention-based graph neural networks to process variable swarm topologies. Under the adopted training setting, the reward and network losses converged within a small number of episodes. Simulation experiments demonstrate successful navigation across different swarm sizes, formations, and planar goal directions. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the transferability of the high-level reference-velocity policy to homogeneous and heterogeneous UAV platforms without fine-tuning. A video of the results is available at https://youtu.be/Ch3ataf1ItQ .

rows.title: Immune Compatible Biohybrid Swarms and Self Repairing Interfaces at the Limit English Publication Description STARLI Flagship 10 30 Physicalized Models 82 Chapters 200 Research Gates Immune Compatible Biohybrid Swarms and Self Repairing Interfaces at the Limit is a high-density research monograph on living cellular actuators joined to synthetic microrobotic swarms. It asks whether hybrid agents can perform pumping and local repair while preserving cell identity, immune compatibility, material traceability, independent stop authority, and complete terminal disposition. The book distinguishes recovered motion from recovered compatibility. Biological healing can restore contractile force while antigen burden, inflammatory signaling, interface damage, identity drift, or shed material continues to rise. Every started culture and device remains in the evidence denominator, including failed actuators, immune excursions, lost modules, and incomplete retrievals. Thirty physicalized models connect muscle force velocity, calcium excitation, fatigue and recovery, cardiac synchrony, neuromuscular control, optogenetics, metabolism, active traction, interfacial fracture, antigen presentation, complement, protein corona, macrophage states, fibrosis, cytokine feedback, identity drift, clonal safety, mass closure, degradation, retrieval, controllability, residual detection, and lifecycle reliability. Eighty-two chapters develop the research architecture through five one-page sections per chapter. Two hundred Research Gates specify matched pure synthetic and pure biological baselines, blinded challenges, paired measurements, adversarial explanations, and pass, fail, abstain, or domain-restriction outcomes. No gate can pass on restored force alone. The monograph remains within controlled in vitro and compliant pretransplant research. It does not infer clinical safety from movement, short-term viability, low bulk cytokine levels, or apparent disappearance after retrieval. Its Phoenix Answer Embryo, the Biohybrid Interface Passport, binds cell source, material identity, immune history, actuation, drift, shed mass, withdrawal, and residual evidence into one auditable record. This volume is intended for researchers in biohybrid robotics, biomaterials, immunoengineering, tissue engineering, microrobotics, cellular biomechanics, control, metrology, and translational manufacturing. It is designed for successor research: its models and gates can be executed, falsified, narrowed, or extended without inheriting hidden culture or operator assumptions. rows.title: MICROROBOTIC SAMPLING AND QUANTUM BIOSENSING CO-DESIGN AT THE LIMIT An Exploratory Engineering Monograph on Sample Handling, Reference Control, and Biological Risk Boundaries This research monograph examines whether controlled micromanipulation can improve the positioning, transport, recovery, and reproducibility of biological research samples without increasing sample alteration, cross-contamination, thermal exposure, or misleading biosensor signals. The guiding three-coupling is Sample Handling × Reference Control × Biological Risk Boundary. Its guiding question is not whether an autonomous microrobot can move a sample, but whether the resulting measurement remains traceable to an authentic, independently verifiable sample state. The work synthesizes three mother research architectures: (S) Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 9–16 and 33–40, for embodied manipulation and collective transport; (QH) Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, especially chapters 9–24 and 67–74, for raw-to-result lineage, uncertainty-aware decisions, human authority and recovery; and (QB) Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 57–73, for fabrication variation, reference transfer, calibration, drift and measurement integrity. These sources contribute methods rather than evidence that the cross-domain integration is already demonstrated. Across 82 chapters and 12 single-section research studies per chapter, the monograph examines non-clinical microfluidic sample environments, magnetic and acoustic micromanipulation, optical and electrokinetic methods, nanoscale surface chemistry, quantum-enabled and classical biosensing, correlated uncertainty, sample-to-signal provenance, authorized closed-loop control, physical damage and carryover detection, interlaboratory replication, lifecycle burden, and successor reconstruction. Thirty mathematical and physical derivation plates introduce assumptions and validity boundaries. Every chapter presents a distinct candidate engineering relation and a geometric three-dimensional research portrait. The validation approach prioritizes synthetic phantoms and permitted ex-vivo research standards in closed non-clinical environments. It calls for blinded comparison of skilled manual pipetting, passive microfluidics, and robotic operation under matched sample identity, measurement time, contamination constraints, and independent calibration. A perceived improvement in robotic throughput or algorithmic readout quality does not establish improved sample authenticity. Any claim of quantum advantage must be compared against an appropriate, strong classical sensing baseline end to end. The research architecture closes with 200 independently framed Research Gates and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos, each accompanied by one of 233 indexed equation eggs. Gates specify questions, comparators, pass criteria, and veto conditions; answer embryos can be challenged, decomposed, recombined or retired. An accompanying Research Gates spreadsheet maps these questions to chapters, physical relations, evidence packets and future experiments. The study is explicitly exploratory and non-clinical. It does not establish the existence of mature autonomous in-body nanorobotic medicine, grant permission for diagnosis or therapy, or imply that quantum-enabled detection is intrinsically superior. Candidate indices and equations are design hypotheses unless identified as established physical relations; many passages use a recurring structured research grammar and require independent experiments, domain expert review, and peer assessment. The aim is to leave a reproducible and falsifiable research architecture that subsequent investigators are free to revise, reject, or extend. Feng Cheng-en (33) × Starli STARLI | Nano–Quantum Tri-Coupling Research Series | Flagship 13

rows.title: NANO–QUANTUM MANUFACTURING ENERGY ECONOMICS AND MAINTENANCE LIFECYCLES AT THE LIMIT Qualified Yield × Resource Burden × Long-Term Maintainability This exploratory flagship research monograph asks whether tri-coupled quantum measurement, nanoscale manufacturing and distributed robot coordination can provide a lower total burden per independently verified accepted output than well-qualified classical, centralized or human-maintained alternatives. The answer must not be decided by the sensitivity of a single sensor, by an isolated peak yield, or by the model loss of an AI quality predictor. The full economic boundary must include equipment capital, cooling and power loads, reference standards, sample and chemical consumption, operator time, calibration and interlaboratory checks, rework and waste, safety recovery, spares and terminal retirement. THREE MOTHER LINEAGES AND THEIR BOUNDARIES. Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit (S), notably chapters 12, 37–40 and 73–80, provides the methodology for distributed logistics, congestion, robotic coordination, maintenance and infrastructure value. Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit (QH), notably chapters 72 and 79–80, contributes bounded operational authority, procurement, fallback, lifecycle continuity and responsible governance; these conceptual methods do not authorize any clinical application. Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit (QB), notably chapters 57–64 and 74–82, contributes calibration traceability, sensor aging, replacement economics and independent quantum/classical benchmark discipline. The cross-book synthesis is an untested research proposal; the mothers do not empirically establish a jointly superior quantum–nano factory. The guiding design ledger is NQ-17: LCC/unit = (C_capex + C_energy + C_cal + C_rework + C_maint + E[C_failure]) / N_accepted. The equation is a candidate accounting heuristic, not a new physical law. A defensible implementation specifies a common time horizon and functional unit, measured input costs, currencies and discounting, joint uncertainty, correlated failures, and whether shared assets and decommissioning are included. Numerators cannot omit technician work, cryogenic or standby power, environmental burden or costly false release. The denominator counts only products or service units meeting independently verified acceptance criteria; an unqualified item or measurement is not an accepted unit. The manuscript contains 82 chapters, each with 12 independently paginated research units; 30 physics and engineering-mathematics derivation plates with validity domains; one core candidate relation and three-dimensional scenario prism per chapter; 200 falsifiable Research Gates; and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. Every Gate and Answer Embryo carries a linked entry in a collection of 233 numbered equation eggs. These are existing relations adapted as research prompts, not 233 newly discovered physical laws or experimentally demonstrated advantages. The long-form research units are partly generated from a shared methodological structure; their total word count does not imply an equivalent volume of independent validated scholarship. COMPARATIVE RESEARCH PROGRAM. Fix the accepted product definition, false-release threshold, energy measurement boundary, reference standards and twelve-month observation horizon. Compare (A) a mature centralized precision line, (B) a distributed swarm assembly line and (C) a hybrid quantum–classical measurement and fabrication architecture. Include independent metrology, maintenance staffing, spares, energy and cooling, consumables, material reuse, qualification and retirement. Perform scenario experiments on electricity price, instrument duty cycle, thermal load, accelerated aging, supplier disruption, network congestion, hidden technician work and joint sensor-reference drift. Where possible, use measured data; otherwise label simulations as simulations and test sensitivity to their assumptions. Long-horizon proof requires direct multi-site evidence and is not supplied by this monograph. The companion Research Gates workbook is an extendable evidence apparatus. It indexes the full chapters, the 30 derivation plates, 200 Gates, 33 answer embryos and 233 equation eggs. It adds a transparent equipment-and-resource ledger, a verified accepted-unit register, maintenance labor register, classical and quantum baseline comparisons, scenario stress tests, sensitivity tracking, uncertainty evaluation, retirement ledger and three-source research lineage. Laboratory teams may mark individual gates as untested, falsified, amended or verified and preserve the provenance of that decision. SCIENTIFIC, ECONOMIC AND REGULATORY LIMITS. rows.abstract: NANO–QUANTUM MANUFACTURING ENERGY ECONOMICS AND MAINTENANCE LIFECYCLES AT THE LIMIT Qualified Yield × Resource Burden × Long-Term Maintainability This exploratory flagship research monograph asks whether tri-coupled quantum measurement, nanoscale manufacturing and distributed robot coordination can provide a lower total burden per independently verified accepted output than well-qualified classical, centralized or human-maintained alternatives. The answer must not be decided by the sensitivity of a single sensor, by an isolated peak yield, or by the model loss of an AI quality predictor. The full economic boundary must include equipment capital, cooling and power loads, reference standards, sample and chemical consumption, operator time, calibration and interlaboratory checks, rework and waste, safety recovery, spares and terminal retirement. THREE MOTHER LINEAGES AND THEIR BOUNDARIES. Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit (S), notably chapters 12, 37–40 and 73–80, provides the methodology for distributed logistics, congestion, robotic coordination, maintenance and infrastructure value. Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit (QH), notably chapters 72 and 79–80, contributes bounded operational authority, procurement, fallback, lifecycle continuity and responsible governance; these conceptual methods do not authorize any clinical application. Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit (QB), notably chapters 57–64 and 74–82, contributes calibration traceability, sensor aging, replacement economics and independent quantum/classical benchmark discipline. The cross-book synthesis is an untested research proposal; the mothers do not empirically establish a jointly superior quantum–nano factory. The guiding design ledger is NQ-17: LCC/unit = (C_capex + C_energy + C_cal + C_rework + C_maint + E[C_failure]) / N_accepted. The equation is a candidate accounting heuristic, not a new physical law. A defensible implementation specifies a common time horizon and functional unit, measured input costs, currencies and discounting, joint uncertainty, correlated failures, and whether shared assets and decommissioning are included. Numerators cannot omit technician work, cryogenic or standby power, environmental burden or costly false release. The denominator counts only products or service units meeting independently verified acceptance criteria; an unqualified item or measurement is not an accepted unit. The manuscript contains 82 chapters, each with 12 independently paginated research units; 30 physics and engineering-mathematics derivation plates with validity domains; one core candidate relation and three-dimensional scenario prism per chapter; 200 falsifiable Research Gates; and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. Every Gate and Answer Embryo carries a linked entry in a collection of 233 numbered equation eggs. These are existing relations adapted as research prompts, not 233 newly discovered physical laws or experimentally demonstrated advantages. The long-form research units are partly generated from a shared methodological structure; their total word count does not imply an equivalent volume of independent validated scholarship. COMPARATIVE RESEARCH PROGRAM. Fix the accepted product definition, false-release threshold, energy measurement boundary, reference standards and twelve-month observation horizon. Compare (A) a mature centralized precision line, (B) a distributed swarm assembly line and (C) a hybrid quantum–classical measurement and fabrication architecture. Include independent metrology, maintenance staffing, spares, energy and cooling, consumables, material reuse, qualification and retirement. Perform scenario experiments on electricity price, instrument duty cycle, thermal load, accelerated aging, supplier disruption, network congestion, hidden technician work and joint sensor-reference drift. Where possible, use measured data; otherwise label simulations as simulations and test sensitivity to their assumptions. Long-horizon proof requires direct multi-site evidence and is not supplied by this monograph. The companion Research Gates workbook is an extendable evidence apparatus. It indexes the full chapters, the 30 derivation plates, 200 Gates, 33 answer embryos and 233 equation eggs. It adds a transparent equipment-and-resource ledger, a verified accepted-unit register, maintenance labor register, classical and quantum baseline comparisons, scenario stress tests, sensitivity tracking, uncertainty evaluation, retirement ledger and three-source research lineage. Laboratory teams may mark individual gates as untested, falsified, amended or verified and preserve the provenance of that decision. SCIENTIFIC, ECONOMIC AND REGULATORY LIMITS. Quantum sensing advantages are not assumed; a strong classical comparator is mandatory. Sensitivity cannot substitute for evidence of successful manufacturing acceptance, repairability, affordability or human control. A favorable expected-cost statistic cannot legitimize unsafe operation, rights violations or the erasure of environmental costs. This is a large exploratory, template-assisted research architecture, not a report of conducted twelve-month trials, validated commercialization, a certified lifecycle inventory, clinical evidence or peer review. Negative results and safe retirement are meaningful outputs. The framework is designed to make future independent attempts easier to replicate or reject.

rows.title: Optimizing robotic swarm based construction tasks
rows.abstract: Social insects in nature such as ants, termites and bees construct their colonies collaboratively in a very efficient process. In these swarms, each insect contributes to the construction task individually showing redundant and parallel behavior of individual entities. But the robotics adaptations of these swarm's behaviors haven't yet made it to the real world at a large enough scale of commonly being used due to the limitations in the existing approaches to the swarm robotics construction. This paper presents an approach that combines the existing swarm construction approaches which results in a swarm robotic system, capable of constructing a given 2 dimensional shape in an optimized manner.

rows.title: PHEROMONE INSPIRED COORDINATION AND AUTONOMOUS RECOVERY NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Works | White Rainbow Scientific Library Feng Cheng-en (33) x STARLI Working Research Review | October 2026 Can a swarm use persistent environmental traces to find damaged agents, distribute recovery work, and preserve useful function without a central dispatcher? More importantly, can it do so without mistaking old traces, forged signals, correlated sensor errors, or repetitive motion for genuine recovery? PHEROMONE INSPIRED COORDINATION AND AUTONOMOUS RECOVERY NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT investigates this problem at the intersection of artificial stigmergy, fault diagnosis, distributed robotics, robust control, and reproducible engineering. It treats a virtual or physically inscribed pheromone-like mark as a measurable, time-dependent information channel—not as a biological pheromone, a verified diagnosis, or permission to manipulate a machine. The monograph develops thirty mathematically varied research routes covering reaction–diffusion and transport, source provenance, spatial uncertainty, causal fault inference, graph connectivity, change-point detection, attack-resistant coordination, task queues, resource-constrained assignment, bounded-control stability, physical safety barriers, environmental cleanup, and long-term drift. Eighty-two chapter dossiers connect these model classes to five separately paginated research perspectives: mechanism and conservation, adverse causal explanations, blinded experimental discrimination, uncertainty and complete-system burden, and failure-aware successor handoff. Its proposed scientific tests compare trace-based control with strong ordinary alternatives, including centralized event buses, explicit direct messages, random exploration, and resource-matched hybrid designs. Success is defined by independent fault attribution and qualified task recovery rather than attractive robot trajectories or unverified collective agreement. Particular attention is paid to trace expiration and revocation, adversarial source forgery, positive-feedback repair storms, congestion at high swarm density, operator override, and the distinction between task reassignment and actual component repair. The research atlas concludes with 200 Research Gates, intended as distinct falsifiable future studies, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos, provisional ideas that may be corrected, split, abandoned, or rebuilt as new evidence becomes available. A companion spreadsheet links formulas, chapters, study units, Gates, embryos, page numbers, and a curated DOI evidence register.

rows.title: PLANETARY AND EXTREME-ENVIRONMENT QUANTUM–NANO OBSERVATORY NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance This exploratory research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for quantum-enabled and classical sensor networks operating in extreme terrestrial and possible off-world environments. It asks how a distributed observatory can remain scientifically useful under contact loss, power scarcity, reference aging, thermal and radiation stress, material degradation, ambiguous physical changes, delayed commands and difficult maintenance. The central criterion is not uninterrupted telemetry but defensible measurement meaning: a raw observation must retain its measurand, units, calibration lineage, time context, uncertainty and revision history or be declared untrustworthy. The work combines three mother research architectures while respecting their evidential limits. Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 65–80, contributes distributed robotics, fault-tolerant task allocation, remote servicing, resource limits and field operations. Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, particularly chapters 43–49 and 58–82, contributes bounded autonomy, fleet metrology, human override, classical fallback, recovery and successor handoff. Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 33–56 and 79–82, contributes network fault isolation, calibration lineage, replayable evidence and common-mode drift detection. Their intersection motivates proposed experiments but does not demonstrate mature planetary quantum–nano observatories. The central three-coupling is Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance. The candidate mission-continuity heuristic R_mission = R_energy × R_reference × R_comm × R_recovery × R_data represents a useful checklist of necessary capabilities but is not a validated physical law. A product of stage reliabilities requires additional independence assumptions. Joint mission survival must account for correlated failures, shared environmental stresses, time-varying hazard rates, depleted resources and common calibration chains. A highly sensitive quantum sensor is not necessarily preferable to a more durable classical instrument once mass, power, packaging, cryogenic or optical stabilization, calibration, data transport and lifecycle cost are included. The monograph contains 82 research chapters with 12 individually paginated study units per chapter, 30 physical and mathematical derivation plates, a distinct candidate research model and spatial network geometry for each chapter, 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each of the 233 research entrances is paired with a numbered mathematical or physical equation egg. These eggs identify known scientific relationships and interpretation boundaries; they are not newly discovered physical laws. The derivation plates are concise research derivation sketches, not complete mathematical monographs. The experimental program proposes chamber and field-analog comparisons across thermal cycling, vibration, pressure, salinity, contamination, radiation-relevant exposure and delayed or interrupted communications. It challenges independent versus common-mode reference failures, expired calibration artifacts, clock desynchronization, partial network partitions, compromised firmware, cold starts, long no-contact intervals and station retirement. Classical-only, frozen-calibration and manual-reviewed workflows are mandatory comparators where appropriate. Bench tests, field qualification and actual lunar, Martian or deep-ocean deployments are distinct evidence levels. This volume does not claim that the integrated system is currently mission-qualified. A 200-Gate research atlas and related spreadsheets support independent laboratories. Gate records specify questions, controlled experiments, independent acceptance and veto criteria, measurement and reference histories, source lineage, energy-data budgets, communication outage tests, fault injections, recoverability, and successor reconstruction. The 33 Answer Embryos remain provisional structures that can be rejected, separated into classical-only alternatives, repaired or reborn. Scientific retirement and no-data states are treated as legitimate results, not failures of intelligence. SCIENTIFIC BOUNDARY. This is a large-scale, partly template-assisted hypothesis and research-design atlas, not a report of completed physical experiments, qualified space hardware, peer-reviewed validation or guaranteed quantum advantage. A high numerical consensus cannot substitute for a reliable external reference. A robust communication protocol cannot repair a lost measurand or improperly calibrated instrument. Any field deployment would require environment-specific engineering qualification, safety review, lawful mission authority, suitable environmental stewardship and independent verification. Back
