rows.title: Quantitative Assessment of Robotic Swarm Coverage
rows.abstract: This paper studies a generally applicable, sensitive, and intuitive error metric for the assessment of robotic swarm density controller performance. Inspired by vortex blob numerical methods, it overcomes the shortcomings of a common strategy based on discretization, and unifies other continuous notions of coverage. We present two benchmarks against which to compare the error metric value of a given swarm configuration: non-trivial bounds on the error metric, and the probability density function of the error metric when robot positions are sampled at random from the target swarm distribution. We give rigorous results that this probability density function of the error metric obeys a central limit theorem, allowing for more efficient numerical approximation. For both of these benchmarks, we present supporting theory, computation methodology, examples, and MATLAB implementation code.

rows.title: RECONFIGURABLE ROBOTIC SWARMS AND CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONAL REGENERATION AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Works | White Rainbow Scientific Library | Flagship 02 Prospective Research Atlas — English Review Edition, October 2026 Can a distributed population of heterogeneous modular robots reconstruct an operationally qualified capability after damage, without treating a newly assembled shape as evidence of restored function? Reconfigurable Robotic Swarms and Continuous Functional Regeneration at the Limit develops an interdisciplinary research program on modular morphology, distributed self-assembly, task-dependent graph structure, mechanical qualification, connector fatigue, recoverable actions, and independent post-reconfiguration verification. Its central proposition is deliberately testable: a swarm may change its topology after losing modules, but it earns the stronger name of functional regeneration only when its restored configuration satisfies the original, independently assessed service requirements and does not conceal emerging hazards or latent joint failures. The monograph distinguishes three often conflated networks: mechanical connections that transmit forces, communication links that transmit information, and power connections that transport energy. It then investigates how graph connectivity, geometric rigidity, elastic stiffness, buckling, frictional contact, thermal dissipation, material fatigue, sensing uncertainty, local negotiation, and safe rollback constrain what an apparently repaired swarm can actually do. A prospective twenty-module testbed provides recurring engineering anchors: bridge, gripping, and sensing-tower tasks, blinded removal of modules, unseen configurations, independent qualification, and strong comparisons with redundant fixed structures and specialist replacement procedures. The research architecture includes thirty mathematically diverse derivation plates, eighty-two chapter-level questions and their five individually paginated study units, two hundred falsifiable Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. The companion spreadsheet links physical models, chapter topics, prospective study cards, provenance, source DOI records, and page references to support future research and AI-assisted scientific handoff. Published robotics literature supplies a source-grounded context for modular reconfigurable mechanisms and fault-aware planning, including external DOI records for reviews and an existing fault-tolerant modular system. The manuscript separates those precedents from its own unexecuted research designs. Its two STARLI mother volumes are listed as conceptual ancestry, not as independent experimental validation. Biological regeneration functions as an analogy for staged assessment of restoration, not as evidence of biomedical efficacy, autonomous human-tissue repair, or indefinite machine life. This is a prospective research-atlas REVIEW EDITION. The mathematical relations, study proposals, design seeds, and acceptance thresholds are not experimentally validated findings. External mathematical review, whole-text DOI auditing, and a stronger editorial review for chapter-level semantic repetition remain necessary before scholarly publication. Negative findings, conventional method superiority, irreversible module retirement, and scientific abstention are legitimate outcomes within this research program. STARLI | 33 | White Rainbow Scientific Library

rows.title: Secure and secret cooperation in robotic swarms
rows.abstract: The importance of swarm robotics systems in both academic research and real-world applications is steadily increasing. However, to reach widespread adoption, new models that ensure the secure cooperation of large groups of robots need to be developed. This work introduces a novel method to encapsulate cooperative robotic missions in an authenticated data structure known as Merkle tree. With this method, operators can provide the "blueprint" of the swarm's mission without disclosing its raw data. In other words, data verification can be separated from data itself. We propose a system where robots in a swarm, to cooperate towards mission completion, have to "prove" their integrity to their peers by exchanging cryptographic proofs. We show the implications of this approach for two different swarm robotics missions: foraging and maze formation. In both missions, swarm robots were able to cooperate and carry out sequential operations without having explicit knowledge about the mission's high-level objectives. The results presented in this work demonstrate the feasibility of using Merkle trees as a cooperation mechanism for swarm robotics systems in both simulation and real-robot experiments, which has implications for future decentralized robotics applications where security plays a crucial role such as environmental monitoring, infrastructure surveillance, and disaster management.

rows.title: SELF-HEALING QUANTUM SENSOR INFRASTRUCTURE AND RECONFIGURABLE MATTER AT THE LIMIT Module Replacement × Calibration Recovery × Service Continuity This exploratory engineering monograph develops a falsifiable research architecture for modular quantum-enabled and classical sensor infrastructure that must continue providing scientifically valid measurements despite component failure, material aging, vendor discontinuity, shared-reference faults and partial loss of maintenance capability. The central question is not whether a network can switch its modules or restart operation. It is whether that network can recover a traceable measurand, independently verify accepted functions, constrain autonomous repair authority and maintain a reliable fallback or retirement path when restoration is impossible or unsafe. The synthesis combines three prior mother architectures while distinguishing inherited methods from unverified integration hypotheses. Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, especially chapters 52–64, contributes modular reconfiguration, robot maintenance, repairability, physical interfaces and quality assurance. Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, especially chapters 41–49 and 75–82, contributes fault isolation, graded authority, service recovery, classical fallback and reconstructible handoffs. Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, especially chapters 49–64, contributes reference integrity, package drift, calibration recovery, common-mode failure detection and replacement continuity. Those original works are methodological sources, not experimental demonstrations of a finished self-healing quantum–nano infrastructure. The proposed core relation is R_post = (F_verified_after/F_required) × P_trace × P_recover. It is a normalized design heuristic rather than a universal physical law or safety certificate. F_verified_after represents the independently confirmed functions following repair; F_required is the explicitly declared essential service scope. P_trace and P_recover describe traceability and verified recovery, respectively. Their possible statistical dependence, calibration uncertainty, hidden physical wear and categorical scientific or safety vetoes must be evaluated separately. A powered-on replacement cannot count as a successful repair when the old measurand cannot be reconstructed, independent calibration is missing or the new connector causes hidden drift. The research program defines the Replace–Recalibrate–Verify–Rollback protocol. Each event preserves the old reference state, instrument serial number, raw observations, material and connector information, authority, operator identity, calibration uncertainty and independent acceptance results. Two coupled maps—physical module topology and calibration-reference dependency graph—make visible how a local intervention can change network measurement interpretation. The project permits repair, partial restoration, classical fallback, safe service reduction, full replacement and responsible retirement as legitimate possible outcomes. The monograph comprises 82 chapters with 12 separately paginated research units per chapter, 30 concise physics and mathematical derivation plates, one candidate chapter relation and spatial reconfiguration model per chapter, 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Every Gate and Embryo is linked to one of 233 numbered equation eggs that draw on recognized relations in probability, mechanics, statistical uncertainty, control and reliability; the equation eggs are not new physical laws. Chapters use a common comparative research grammar, so programmatically counted words should not be confused with an equal quantity of independent scientific discoveries or fully proved theorems. Proposed experiments compare qualified manual replacement, centralized maintenance, fixed spare-node redundancy and distributed robotic repair with a matched classical-only sensing baseline. A module network is challenged through connector damage, alignment drift, thermal fatigue, forged component identity, expired reference artifacts, firmware regressions, power loss and common-mode calibration failure. Blinded replacement batches and independent laboratory replays evaluate scientific recovery and lifecycle burden rather than merely counting restored packets or achieving low machine-learning loss. The Research Gates workbook provides chapter and page navigation, 200 falsifiable studies, 33 provisional Answer Embryos, physics-plate and equation-egg indices, a module replacement register, calibration lineage, fault injection matrix, recovery closeout, human authority, lifecycle economics and three-source continuity. It is intended as an extendable research apparatus for successor investigators, not as evidence that the listed experiments have been performed. SCIENTIFIC AND DEPLOYMENT BOUNDARIES. No claim is made that quantum sensing is always superior to qualified classical alter

SWARM ASSEMBLY OF QUANTUM DEVICES AND RECONFIGURABLE MATTER AT THE LIMIT A Nano-Quantum Manufacturing Tri-Coupling Research Monograph This exploratory monograph develops a falsifiable engineering program for the distributed assembly, inspection, replacement, and reconfiguration of modular quantum-device test fixtures. rows.abstract: SWARM ASSEMBLY OF QUANTUM DEVICES AND RECONFIGURABLE MATTER AT THE LIMITA Nano-Quantum Manufacturing Tri-Coupling Research Monograph This exploratory monograph develops a falsifiable engineering program for the distributed assembly, inspection, replacement, and reconfiguration of modular quantum-device test fixtures. It integrates three established strands of research architecture: swarm manufacturing and robotic matter; metrologically traceable, bounded quantum-enabled infrastructure; and self-calibrating quantum biosensing networks. Their coupling is organized around Local Operations x Quantum Device Tolerances x Distributed Quality Assurance. The central question is whether cooperative robots and reconfigurable manufacturing cells can lower the full cost and effort of qualified quantum-device assembly without sacrificing optical alignment, electrical continuity, thermal stability, sample integrity, reproducible readout, or provenance. The monograph avoids presuming that quantum effects improve robotic coordination or that generic self-reconfiguring robotic matter is already feasible. Its minimal proposed demonstrator is a modular quantum test-fixture cell with repeatable docking datums, traceable optical-electrical interfaces, reversible component replacement, independently replayable acceptance tests, and explicitly limited agent authority. A major methodological distinction concerns yield. The convenient product of alignment, interconnect, thermal, and traceability rates is not a reliable estimate of total acceptance whenever those outcomes share causes or are statistically dependent. Accordingly, the study uses joint acceptance events and conditional probabilities, records rework as a versioned state transition, and separates first-pass yield from final accepted yield, scrap, energy, inspection, and salvage costs. The same qualified specimens and release thresholds must be used when comparing a single high-precision station, a two-agent cooperative cell, and a multi-agent production cell. The research architecture comprises 82 chapters arranged across physical interfaces, modular geometries, task allocation, optical and cryogenic packaging, uncertainty propagation, calibration transfer, failure injection, repair, security, production economics, and cross-laboratory reconstruction. Eleven structured research units are presented for each chapter. Thirty introductory physics and mathematics plates give relations, derivation steps, assumptions, and experimental validity limits. Chapter-opening geometric studies use three-dimensional isometric representations of modular docking and inspection interfaces. The closing research atlas consists of 200 Research Gates, followed by 33 provisional Answer Embryos. Each of these 233 entrances includes an indexed mathematical “equation egg” intended as a test prompt, not as a newly discovered physical law. The work is deliberately conservative about evidence and autonomy. Raw measurements are separated from calibration adjustments and AI-generated estimates. Shared-reference and common-mode failures are treated as threats to trustworthy agreement among inspection nodes. Every favorable result must be tested against strong classical and centralized alternatives, with matched quality thresholds, uncertainty intervals, energy accounting, human override, and recovery after injected faults. A finding that centralized precision remains superior is a valid and informative research outcome. This is a programmatically expanded, high-volume exploratory research manuscript. Its recurring analytic framework enables systematic comparison between chapters but also introduces repeated structure; it should not be mistaken for an equivalent volume of independent experimental discoveries or for a peer-reviewed manufacturing standard. No autonomous clinical intervention, general-purpose robotic matter capability, or quantum advantage is asserted. The proposed architectures require independent physical experiments, expert review, full uncertainty budgets, and application-specific safety qualification before real deployment. The accompanying Research Gates Excel atlas links chapter references, research questions, comparators, failure boundaries, page numbers, measurement protocols, candidate formula prompts, and future evidence fields. It is intended to support critical review, replicability, negative-result preservation, research handoff, and subsequent concept-fission studies. Source lineages (user-supplied mother volumes):- Swarm Manufacturing & Robotic Matter at the Limit, especially Chapters 41-64.- Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, especially Chapters 58-66.- Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, especially Chapters 57-64. External metrological anchors include the JCGM Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (https://www.bipm.org/en/committees/jc/jcgm/publications), NIST's metrological traceability guidance (https://www.nist.gov/calibrations/traceability), and the 2025 review "Advanced Optical Integration Processes for Photonic-Integrated Circuit Packaging" (https://doi.org/10.1002/admt.202401848). These references inform the limits of the synthesis; they do not validate the newly proposed combined apparatus. STARLI / WHITE RAINBOW CIVILIZATION RESEARCH SERIES

rows.title: SWARM METROLOGY AND AUTONOMOUS REPAIR REQUALIFICATION AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Works | White Rainbow Scientific Library Prospective Research Review Edition | October 2026 A robotic swarm can repair a structure, repeat a successful movement, and agree on a measurement while still misunderstanding the repaired object's physical condition. This monograph explores a deeper engineering question: can distributed measuring agents independently requalify repaired geometry, material properties, and functional capacity when their sensors may share a drifting reference, a common software defect, or an unobservable state? The proposed research programme couples distributed metrology, traceable repair evidence, and independent adjudication. Its mathematical foundation addresses correlated sensor errors, marginalization of calibration bias, measurement observability, covariance intersection, robust estimation, confidence and coverage, sequential decisions, conformity assessment, calibration genealogy, and long-horizon reliability. Thirty distinct mathematical signposts link physical assumptions, measured units, falsifiable predictions, and proposed experiments. Rather than treating sensor consensus as physical truth, the work requires a blind external witness capable of defeating a preferred interpretation. Across 82 research chapters and 410 separately paginated study units, the atlas investigates hidden common-mode calibration faults, coordinate-frame and timestamp drift, non-Gaussian measurement noise, blind regions, firmware contamination, robot-sensor attrition, cross-modal references, release guard bands, and second-laboratory reproducibility. Each chapter specifies measurable quantities, a controlled intervention, a strong conventional comparator, and a research stop condition. Two hundred Research Gates invite future researchers to conduct discriminating experiments under real resource budgets and genuine uncertainty. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos outline revisable concepts that can be corrected, rejected, divided, or rebuilt by successor teams. A separate Excel companion cross-references formulas, chapters, studies, Gates, source DOI metadata, and PDF pages. External references include metrology standards, distributed estimation research, and modular robotics literature; earlier STARLI research works serve only as conceptual genealogy.
